claims.text: Ambient-temperature additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloys produces steep thermal gradients.
Rapid cooling and steep thermal gradients produce elevated residual stresses in additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.
Residual stresses promote fabrication-induced defects in these components.
Build-chamber preheating moderates the rapid cooling and thermal cycles inherent in additive manufacturing.
Build-chamber preheating reduces the temperature differential between the melt pool and surrounding material.
Reducing the melt-pool temperature differential decreases thermal contraction and residual-stress buildup.
Lower thermal gradients and residual stresses produce a more homogeneous microstructure.
Build-chamber preheating reduces porosity relative to an ambient-temperature build.
Build-chamber preheating reduces microcracking relative to an ambient-temperature build.
Build-chamber preheating improves dimensional precision relative to an ambient-temperature build.
Build-chamber preheating enhances tensile strength relative to an ambient-temperature build.
Build-chamber preheating enhances ductility relative to an ambient-temperature build.
Optimized preheating may improve dimensional consistency by roughly 15–25%.
Optimized preheating may reduce fabrication-induced defects by roughly 15–25%.
PBF-LB and laser-directed energy deposition are viable additive-manufacturing routes for compositionally complex alloys.
The proposed preheating intervention should be effective for CoCrFeNiMn and AlCoCrFeNi alloys.
Compositionally complex alloys can be additively manufactured from either pre-alloyed powders or elemental-powder blends.
The magnitude of the preheating benefit varies with alloy composition, machine configuration, and preheating temperature.
Systems with existing thermal control will obtain only marginal gains from chamber preheating.
An optimized preheating temperature can slow cooling without adversely affecting melt-pool dynamics.
